title: Are Your Customers Unhappy? Would You Know If They Were?
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Joel Trammell opens with a story about a Tesla air conditioner repair that went wrong and then was fixed because someone actually read his customer survey and had the authority to act. He uses it to argue that most CEOs only believe they know how customers feel, and that unless feedback machinery reaches them they live in a bubble. His proposed diagnostic is to ask the leadership team once a quarter how many times the company heard about disappointing a customer, treating a zero as cause for alarm. He explains why Customer Success should not report to sales: the sales leader is paid for bookings and momentum, so bad news gets softened and the function drifts toward account management. Because customer problems often span product, sales and pricing, only the CEO has the view to diagnose and resolve them. He closes with practical steps, including measuring the leader on retention and customer outcomes and having the CEO call customers directly.
points: A quarterly question to the leadership team, how many times did we hear about disappointing a customer, exposes whether bad news is reaching the top, and a zero should worry a CEO.
Customers rarely complain when disappointed; they disengage and later cite budget, so by the time it reaches the CEO as churn it is too late.
Placing Customer Success under sales creates an incentive to soften bad news and turns the function into renewal and upsell management.
Customer problems usually span product, sales promises and pricing, so only the CEO has the cross-functional view to resolve them.
Practical steps include measuring the Customer Success leader on retention and outcomes, keeping a running count of customer letdowns, and letting the team escalate without permission.
quotes: Most CEOs think they know how their customers feel. That is usually a comforting belief that isn’t quite true.
A big number is uncomfortable, but it tells you the news is getting through and you can do something about it. A zero should really worry you.
Most of the time, customers won’t tell you when you disappoint them. They just move on and engage less.
It’s not that the sales leader is hiding customer dissatisfaction on purpose. But when your boss’s bonus depends on the story being good, the story gets softer.
A customer can renew for two years out of inertia and be unhappy the whole time. A good Customer Success function reads between those lines.
No single function is equipped on its own to diagnose the issue and decide on the proper resolution. It requires the CEO’s 10,000-foot view.
Keep a running count of every time a customer was let down and review it monthly. If it’s suspiciously empty, be suspicious.
